title: The -a flag, and the file it silently leaves behind
summary: git commit -a feels like 'commit everything'. It is not. Find the gap the hard way, then learn the habit that closes it.
mental_model: `-a` means 'stage every *tracked* file that changed'. A brand-new file has never been tracked, so it is invisible to `-a` — and to the commit you thought was complete.

steps.title: A change split across an old file and a new one
steps.why: pump.py was modified and now imports limits.py, which is brand new. Logically this is one change. Git sees two very different kinds of file.

steps.title: Commit with -a and feel good about it
steps.why: It succeeds, reports a file changed, and looks complete. Nothing warns you that half the change was left behind.
steps.expect: One file in the commit: pump.py. limits.py is nowhere.

steps.title: Find the break
steps.why: The committed tree imports a module that does not exist in it. On your machine everything works, because the file is sitting there untracked. In CI, it is an ImportError.
steps.expect: HEAD contains an import of limits, but no limits.py.

steps.title: Prove it the way CI would
steps.why: `git stash -u` sets your working tree to exactly what the commit contains. This is the cheapest possible way to see your commit through someone else's eyes before you push it.
steps.expect: limits.py vanishes while stashed — that is the state you just committed.

steps.title: Fix it into the same commit
steps.why: `git add -A` stages everything including new and deleted files. Amending folds it into the existing commit so history never records the broken state.

verify.label: both files are in the commit

steps.title: The habit that prevents it
steps.why: Run `git status --short` and `git diff --staged` before every commit. Two seconds, and it catches this class of mistake along with stray debug lines and accidentally staged secrets.

verify.label: the commit contains the whole change, new file included
verify.hint: -a skips untracked files; git add -A does not

verify.label: it was folded into the existing commit, not tacked on as a fixup
nothing left behind in the working tree

pitfalls: `git commit -am "msg"` is the same trap with fewer keystrokes. New files are still skipped.
`-a` also stages deletions of tracked files, which is occasionally a surprise in the other direction.
`git add .` stages the current directory downwards only. From a subdirectory it quietly misses changes elsewhere; `git add -A` does not.
A CI job that runs from a fresh clone is the honest test of whether your commit is complete.
cheatsheet: stage modified TRACKED files, then commit
stage everything: new, modified and deleted
stage from the current directory down
temporarily see your tree exactly as committed
